summary: The board logic that matters is the CRU write/read decode, and it is a near line-by-line transliteration of MAME's cosmicg_output_w / port_0_r / port_1_r. The state names match (March_Select, Gun_Die, Sound_EN), each offset has the same case, the gun/die sample choice is the same, and so is the sound-enable stop-all. Sound is MAME's sample set triggered through a generic sample player, and the ROM load applies MAME's dummy-instruction hack at 0x1E9F. The video path is a per-pixel fetch/latch/shift pipeline driven by raster counters, which is mildly hardware-like. But the board's MC6845 CRTC is not modelled at all: free-running counters with ad-hoc constants replace it, so the timing does not come from the board. That leaves the core with no chip-level structure of its own.

findings.signal: CRU write decode transliterates MAME output handler
findings.note: A case on CRU offset 2..15 has the same per-offset behaviour as MAME's switch: 2 = march sound indexed by March_Select, 3/4/5 set march-select bits, 7 = stop-then-restart, 8 = stop on 0, 10 = flip, 11 = watchdog, 12 = sound enable with stop-all, 14 = gun/die select. Every action is gated by sound-enable, just as MAME checks m_sound_enabled.

findings.signal: MAME state variable names and sample-selection logic
findings.note: The signals March_Select, Gun_Die and Sound_EN mirror MAME's member variables. Offset 13 picks trigger 12 or 13 from Gun_Die, which is exactly MAME's 13 - gun_die_select sample index rather than a discrete-sound circuit.

findings.signal: Sound is MAME's sample model, not the board's discrete/NE556 circuits
findings.note: SoundTrigger/SoundStop bit vectors start and stop numbered WAV samples (march pitches 0-7, attack, bonus...). This is MAME's samples_device start/stop/loop abstraction, not the board's analog sound.

During download the word at byte address 0x1E9F is forced to x"04C0". This is the same location MAME patches with its 'convert dummy instruction' hack, a software fix with no counterpart on the board.

findings.signal: Process split mirrors MAME CRU address map handlers
findings.note: The CRU read is one case on address(15:4) = 0/1 that selects bit 'ki' of port 0 (four counter bits plus in0) or port 1 (in1 plus DIPs). This matches MAME's two read handlers and their offset>=4 split, not a modelled 74LS251-style mux structure.

findings.signal: MC6845 CRTC replaced by ad-hoc counters
findings.note: Neither the board nor MAME is followed. hcnt reloads to 0x0AB and vcnt to 0x0F8, with fixed blank/sync compares, and the CPU-visible CRTC registers at 0x3FF0-7 are not decoded. Raster timing therefore comes from neither the board's CRTC programming nor MAME's 6845 model.

findings.signal: Vertical position readback substitutes for CRTC MA lines
findings.note: CRU bits 0-3 return vcnt(7:4), with zero outside the active half, instead of the 6845's MA8-MA11. This is a functional stand-in that matches neither the hardware's lines nor MAME's call.

VRAM and colour-PROM addresses are issued at hcnt(2:0)=101 for the next character. Data is latched at 111, then shifted one bit per pixel clock. This differs from MAME's per-row MC6845 update-row loop, but it is only weak evidence because any FPGA bitmap core would do the same.

findings.signal: Colour output as resistor weighting rather than MAME palette rule
findings.note: Red is built as bit0 driving the '1010' weight plus bit3 driving '0101', so the two bits add like a resistor ladder. MAME instead forces 0xFF whenever the index is above 8. There is also an optional blue background with no counterpart in the MAME pen table.

findings.signal: ROM data-pin swap and colour-PROM addressing
findings.note: The ROM bit reorder is the pin-swap any correct core must apply. The colour-PROM address page & V(7:4) & H(7:4) is the same lookup MAME computes. Both are required shared knowledge.

The 0000-1FFF ROM / 2000-3FFF RAM decode matches the required map. The coin raises interrupt level 4 through an edge latch cleared by int_ack. That is an FPGA convenience that models neither the board's NE556 nor MAME's level-follow.
